title: A hymn in Vadhans
hookLine: a wedding song about a horse and a lament that begins with praise, a few pages apart

lines: A HORSE IN A LANE OF LIGHTS.
cards: What's the first word of a funeral song? In Guru Nanak's laments in Raga Vadhans, it's blessed.

A few pages earlier in the same raga, the music is for a different scene: a horse groomed and saddled in a lane strung with lights, relatives singing, the groom climbing on, the drum starting up. Today, one song of each.

teach.h: GHORIAN: THE BODY IS THE MARE.
teach.b: First, the wedding. Guru Ram Das's ghorian, the songs of the wedding horse, start with a surprise of their own. The horse isn't a horse.
In plain English: this body is the mare, and the Lord made it. Blessed is the human body, the song says, gained by good fortune.
Then it puts on the saddle of understanding what is good, and rides the mare across the hard road toward the Lord. The groom's ride to the bride's home becomes the soul's ride toward God.
Anyone who has seen a groom set out has the picture already; the Guru only changes who's riding where. Now the lament.

Guru Nanak's alahnian open, in plain English: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the whole world to its tasks. A mourning song that starts by praising the One who made the order the death belongs to.

Later the alahnian say it plainly: whoever comes must rise and go. That's not cold comfort. It sets the grief inside the Creator's order instead of outside it, so the mourners aren't left alone with it.
Put the two side by side. Both are about leaving: a groom leaves to begin a household; a soul leaves this world. Both are about a journey toward the Lord.
And both are sung in Vadhans. The Gurus didn't need one sound for celebration and another for loss.
The same music walks with a family through both doors.

how: Guru Ram Das's ghorian and Guru Nanak's alahnian are both sung in Raga Vadhans; the ghorian are associated with weddings and the alahnian with mourning, and both turn the occasion toward remembrance of God.

games.q: what does “a hymn in vadhans” mean?
o: a hymn sung only when a child is born
a ballad about a Guru's journey on horseback
the wedding-horse song and the lament, in one raga

games.q: who wrote what in vadhans — tap the pairs.

s: in the ghorian, the horse is just a horse
the body is the mare, made by the Lord, saddled with understanding and ridden toward God.
Guru Nanak's laments open by praising the Creator
blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the world to its tasks.
the Granth keeps wedding songs and laments in separate ragas

games.q: you're writing a lament for a family that has lost someone. how does Guru Nanak's begin?
o: with a cry of anger at death.
with blessing the Creator who set the world to its tasks.
with the name of the one who died.
games.why: the alahnian open with praise and later say whoever comes must rise and go, setting grief inside the Creator's order.

practice: With each in-breath, think of a beginning you've witnessed, a wedding, a birth, a first day; with each out-breath, an ending, a goodbye, a funeral, a last visit, and notice it's one breath doing both.
If you pray, say Waheguru at the turn of each breath. If an ending is still raw and heavier than you can carry, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Vadhans. Guru Ram Das's wedding-horse song, where the body is the mare, and Guru Nanak's lament, which opens by blessing the Creator. Today's word.

orig.note: ghorian, songs of the wedding horse; in Guru Ram Das's, the body is the mare.

carryVoice: Your line: the same raga for both. A body as the mare, and a lament that opens with blessed. Until tomorrow.
